title: Vertical 3D charge-coupled shift-register memory with one regenerator per string
idea: Po: the bit is a rumor passed down a line. Store charge packets in potential wells along a tall vertical channel with dozens of stacked gate layers (3D NAND-like tiers clocked as a CCD); packets shift up and down and only the end-of-string regenerating sense amp restores them, so refresh is the shifting itself, with no per-bit capacitor or access transistor.
why: Facts 2, 4 and 7: reuses 3D NAND tier deposition (no EUV per tier, density scales with tier count); access becomes 100 ns-1 us block access, suited to tensor streams.
note: 3D NAND tiers clocked as a CCD avoid per-bit transistors; poly-Si transfer efficiency, dark current and serial access are doubts.

title: Legacy-node always-on island lets modern DRAM fully power down
idea: Put a 32-64 MB refresh-free die on the package (180 nm thick-oxide or loadless cells) holding page tables, kernel and wake state. Modern DRAM banks then enter deep power-down with no refresh when idle, flushing or discarding their contents.
why: Idle refresh power (16-33%) goes to near zero for phones and lightly loaded servers, and U.S. legacy fabs make the island.

title: Antiferroelectric latent-charge buffer holds stored-1 voltage on a plateau
idea: Reverse the capacitor dielectric's role from passive to defending its charge: use ZrO2-rich antiferroelectric HZO and bias the plate so a stored '1' sits just above the AFE back-switching voltage. As leakage drains the node, AFE domains switch back and release bound polarization charge (~10-20 uC/cm2), pinning the voltage on a plateau the way latent heat holds ice water at 0 C.
why: Retention and charge wall (facts 1, 3): effective capacitance at the hold point rises 5-10x, so retention rises ~5x without taller pillars; AFE has no remanent polarization, avoiding the fatigue/imprint of prior HZO FeRAM concepts.
note: AFE back-switching plateau multiplies effective hold capacitance; AFE endurance far below 1e15 and nm-scale domain granularity are doubts.

title: Lossy NUMA node standard: OS pages tagged by error tolerance
idea: Push a JEDEC/CXL descriptor that publishes each region's raw-BER-vs-refresh curve, plus a Linux 'lossy NUMA node' reached with mmap(MAP_LOSSY). KV caches, media buffers and caches go to 1%-BER regions refreshed rarely; kernel and databases stay on fully protected memory.
why: Supply and fact 3: makes 1%-BER memory a standard, procurable class so the other tolerance tricks deploy across vendors; government AI-cluster procurement can require support.

title: One global clock restores every cell: gated-diode charge-pump bistables
idea: Inverts 'refresh is done row by row by sense amps': each cell is a gated diode (large capacitance when inverted, small when depleted) tied to a shared plate clock and a diode to the supply; a stored '1' couples the clock strongly and is topped up each cycle while a '0' couples weakly and stays below the diode threshold, so one global clock refreshes billions of cells at once.
why: Lets cheap leaky TFT or poly cells work with no row refresh, sense-amp refresh path or refresh controller (fact 7), ~2 devices per cell in low-mask tiers, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: continuous clock power and margin between stable points.
note: Global clock tops up only stored 1s, letting leaky TFT cells skip row refresh; doubt: continuous clock power and bistable margins across billions of cells.

title: Coaxial nested capacitor shells: four cells in one hole
idea: IFR: one hole holds many cells. Conformally deposit four concentric storage electrodes separated by high-k and plate shells in one deep hole, each ending at a different height so a ring-shaped oxide-TFT access device wraps each shell's exposed top edge at its own level; one etch plus depositions makes four cells per hole.
why: Constraint: 4 cells per 4F^2 hex hole is ~6x versus 6F^2 planar, and a second hole tier reaches ~12x with mostly deposition steps; ultralow-leak ring TFTs offset the smaller per-shell capacitance.
note: Four shells per hole could give ~6x density; per-shell capacitance and staggered ring TFTs are the doubts.

title: Crested-barrier capacitor: the capacitor is its own access switch
idea: Inverts 'storage and switch are separate devices': each crossbar node is a floating metal nanolayer between two crested tunnel barriers (e.g., nitride/AlN/nitride trilayers) whose peak collapses at high field, giving ~10^12 current change between the ~3 V write and ~1 V hold; charge on the floating layer is the bit, written in ns by tunneling and read capacitively, from one blanket deposition per deck.
why: No transistor, no capacitor tower, one deposition per deck in 4F2 crossbar stacks, ~100x cheaper per GB; crested barriers reduce oxide stress, aiming at 10^12+ endurance; trade-off: write energy and unproven endurance.
note: Transistor-free, capacitor-tower-free 4F2 decks from blanket depositions would cut cost/bit >10x; doubt: capacitive crossbar readout and 1e12 write/hold contrast.

title: Optane's selector drift turned into DRAM retention
idea: In 3D XPoint, the ovonic threshold switch's threshold voltage drifted upward with log-time after each firing, which eroded read margins. Use two back-to-back OTS films as the access device of a crosspoint 1S1C capacitor cell. After each access the threshold drifts up, so the selector's off-state leakage falls as the stored bit ages. Each access or refresh re-fires the selector, which resets its state.
why: Transistor-free, stackable 4F2 crosspoint DRAM (attacks the 3D DRAM blocker and litho cost). Because drift makes leakage fall over time instead of sitting at a fixed tail, refresh is claimed to be ~10x longer than in half-select-limited crosspoint designs.
note: Drift-as-feature is clever, but OTS off-leakage sits ~1e6x above fA retention needs; stackable transistorless DRAM if solved.

title: Thousand tiny tapeouts: crowdsourced access-device leakage variants on open PDKs
idea: 10-person constraint: crowdsource the search a small team cannot fund. Publish an open eDRAM access-device test-cell template for open-PDK shuttles (SKY130, GF180, IHP SG13G2). Pay bounties to hobbyists and students whose variants (gate shapes, well-bias tricks, guard rings, stacked devices) beat the baseline in silicon-measured retention, ranked by an automated FPGA tester.
why: Fact 3: hundreds of cheap parallel experiments explore leakage geometry faster than one team could, and the winners feed tail-reduction techniques into licensable IP.
note: Open-PDK 130-180 nm leakage physics transfers poorly to DRAM access devices.

title: Retired hyperscale DIMMs re-certified with a per-module retention passport
idea: Second-hand DRAM has not won trust because buyers cannot see a module's wear or retention. A test cell measures each retired DIMM's retention tail at temperature and writes a module-specific refresh multiplier and a weak-row list into its SPD. Modules with leakier access transistors then run at 2x refresh instead of being scrapped.
why: Raises usable memory supply through recycling during a ~4x price spike, handling the leakage tail with per-module refresh instead of discard.

title: Diode-steered capacitor stack: one transistor, sixteen bits per pillar
idea: IFR: one switch serves a whole tower of bits. Deposit 16 plate-electrode/dielectric tiers around one vertical storage pillar, with a thin oxide Schottky diode in each tier between plate and capacitor, so a plate-line pulse forward-biases only the selected tier onto the shared pillar node, read through a single access transistor; tiers come from deposition and one hole etch.
why: Constraint: 16 bits per 4F^2 footprint is ~24x the bits of 6F^2 planar at ~1.5-2x wafer cost, about 10x bits per dollar; it also removes 15 of 16 access transistors and their leakage tail.
note: 16 bits per pillar from deposition plus one hole etch; doubt: ~0.2 fF per tier capacitance and diode disturb on shared node.

title: Memory on window glass: multi-tier oxide TFT cells on display lines
idea: Inverts 'memory is made on 300 mm silicon wafers': run 1T1C cells on idle Gen-8.5 to Gen-10.5 LCD/OLED glass lines, stacking 10-20 tiers with KrF-class litho at ~0.3 um and oxide-TFT access whose ultralow leakage lets tiny capacitors skip refresh; dice panels into tiles bonded to a small CMOS controller.
why: Display glass costs ~100-1000x less per area than leading-edge silicon; at 20 tiers and 4F2, ~$0.1-0.4/GB, ~25-100x cheaper; trade-off is ~100 ns-1 us access and lower density per volume.
note: Gen-10.5 glass is cheap per area; 20 tiers at 0.3 um could approach <$0.5/GB, but 100 ns-1 us access makes it capacity-tier, not DRAM.
